item.title: Ranking honeybee breeder colonies: a probabilistic method using vine copulas to consider multiple criteria
item.description: arXiv:2611.31322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ranking honeybee colonies according to multiple performance criteria is central to selection in bee breeding, but deterministic scores provide limited information about how a selected colony compares with the population of available colonies. We propose a population-calibrated probabilistic score based on a weighted Euclidean distance to an ideal colony and an estimation of the joint distribution of the data. For a candidate colony, the probability-score is the probability that a colony drawn from a reference population outperforms the candidate. We estimate the dependence structure among criteria using a vine copula after apiary-specific rank transformations, allowing different marginal distributions while modelling a common dependence structure. Importantly, the joint distribution calibrates the distance into a probability but does not change the ordering induced by a fixed distance and weight vector. We apply the method to 265 observations from eight French and Italian apiaries during the 2024 and 2025 seasons. Dependence among the four criteria is weak in this dataset, and the vine-copula and independence probability-scores are therefore similar. A simulation study evaluates probability-score estimation under a range of dependence structures, while bootstrap and apiary-subset analyses quantify sensitivity to sampling and study composition. We additionally assess preference robustness by evaluating the proportion of admissible weight vectors for which a colony belongs to the top ranking. The framework provides an interpretable and reproducible population-relative score for multi-criteria colony selection.

item.title: Turbulent Epidemics: Scale-dependent Fluctuations as a Probe of Population Heterogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2611.31334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heterogeneous dynamics, including phenomena such as superspreading and clustering, is a hallmark of many infectious diseases. A key challenge lies in identifying observables that constrain heterogeneous dynamics. We here adapt the technique of turbulence decomposition from fluid dynamics to extract scale-dependent fluctuation spectra and correlation functions from disaggregated epidemiological data as a probe of population heterogeneity. To investigate possible explanations for the observed heterogeneities during the COVID-19 winter wave in Germany in 2020/21, we calculate synthetic observables using the new network-based simulation code \textsc{Epimetheus} for an idealized structured population. The code can flexibly incorporate clustering, heterogeneous connectivity and susceptibility, superspreading as well as temporal modulations of transmission risk and factors like waning of immunity and vaccination. A qualitative comparison of simulated and observed fluctuation spectra and correlation functions as well as the secondary attack rate and the overdispersion indicates that both clustering and variations of susceptibility across population substructures of all scales are required to produce the observed dynamics. Combined with heterogeneous connectivity, it is likely that self-limiting effects would have limited the winter outbreak to $0.2\texttt{-}0.35$ of the population without further behavioral changes after the autumn of 2020. A uniform population-wide reduction of transmission risk alone does not adequately explain the observed heterogeneities. Further analysis of the relative contributions and interplay of interventions and self-limiting effects on COVID-19 disease dynamics is required. We outline avenues towards a better integration of heterogeneity in models for predicting infectious disease dynamics and diagnosing effects of interventions.
item.dc:creator: Bernhard Mueller, Michael Lorke, M. Gabriela M. Gomes, Inken Padberg

item.title: Evolutionary constraints on protein fold diversity
item.description: arXiv:2611.33104v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Arrangements of secondary structures in proteins yield a wide variety of possible topologies, yet the protein folds observed in nature are limited in their diversity. Is the number of protein folds limited by biophysical constraints or by evolutionary contingency? In recent years, the development of new methods for protein structure prediction and comparison, molecular design, and the rapid progress of cryo-electron microscopy revealed new insights into the protein fold space. Here, we present recent findings demonstrating that natural proteins adopt only a small fraction of all possible folds and discuss how evolutionary processes limit the diversity of evolving protein folds.
item.dc:creator: Harutyun Sahakyan, Eugene V. Koonin

item.title: Coexistence and extinction in stochastic Lotka--Volterra systems with Volterra--Lyapunov stable interactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.28174v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider stochastic Lotka-Volterra systems $dX=\mathrm{Diag}(X)(\alpha+AX)dt+\mathrm{Diag}(X)\Gamma\,dB$ with nondegenerate noise and a Volterra-Lyapunov stable interaction matrix $A$, that is, $DA+A^\top D\prec0$ for some positive diagonal matrix $D$. This class covers every self-limited predator-prey food web that is conservative in the sense of Volterra, in particular every such web whose interaction graph is a forest. Let $\beta=\alpha-\frac12\mathrm{diag}(\Gamma\Gamma^\top)$ be the vector of noise-corrected growth rates and $m=-A^{-1}\beta$. We show that the process has a stationary distribution under which all species have positive densities if and only if $m>0$. In that case the process is strongly stochastically persistent, and its stationary distribution is unique and has mean $m$. When $m>0$ fails, the species that survive are those present in the unique saturated nonnegative equilibrium $\bar x$ of the deterministic system $\dot x=\mathrm{Diag}(x)(\beta+Ax)$. Almost surely, the occupation measures converge to the stationary distribution of this subcommunity, and $\log X_i(t)/t$ converges to $(\beta+A\bar x)_i\le0$ for every species $i$. The proofs rely on the theory of invasion rates of Hening and Nguyen. For Lotka-Volterra systems, invasion rates are affine in the mean of the underlying measure. Combined with two quadratic identities, this provides explicit weights $Dm$ for their persistence theorem and identifies the limiting regime when persistence fails, without enumerating the invariant measures on the boundary.
item.dc:creator: Jorge Ramirez Osorio
